title: The Atlas keeps 'Executive' and 'Spell' as strictly separate terms because they name authority and artifact
content:
A.1.11.1.2.2 states plainly that "the terms 'Executive' and 'Spell' are distinct concepts" and then fixes four terms:

- **Executive / Executive Vote** — "used in all instances where the formal governance vote is being referenced."
- **Executive Process** — the end-to-end development of an Executive Vote, involving Facilitators, Spell teams (collectively the "Governance Security Engineering Team") and other recognized Ecosystem Actors.
- **Spell** — "the smart contract that executes the changes to the protocol approved by Sky Governance in an Executive Vote," used when referring to code base, code operations, reviews and quality.
- **Spell process** — the end-to-end development of a Spell by the Core Facilitator and current Spell team, with **Spell development process** as the narrower technical subset.

The distinction is not pedantry; it separates *authority* from *artifact*, and each has a different failure mode and a different accountable group. A vote can be legitimate while its Spell is defective, and a Spell can be technically flawless while executing something never authorized.

Much of the surrounding emergency machinery depends on holding the two apart. Standby Spells exist because a valid decision can be blocked by the cost of producing a Spell; Core GovOps' authenticity validation exists because the artifact may not match the authority it claims; and Protego exists to cancel an artifact whose authority has since been repudiated.
description: Executive Vote is the formal governance vote; Spell is the smart contract that executes what it approved — each with its own end-to-end process and its own participants.
